How to maximize your returns?

Don’t just chase higher risk-reward ratios, focus on the probability of your stop being hit.

You have to think in expected values rather than absolute RR.

A 1 to 10 RR with a wide stop isn’t necessarily worse than a 1 to 20 RR setup with a tight stop.

The tighter your stop, the faster your hit rate decreases, and it doesn’t decrease linearly but exponentially due to the inherent variance of the market.

Instead, think in expected values: 

Expected value = (Reward × Hitrate) - (Loss × (1 - Hitrate) )

Consider these scenarios:  
10R with a 60% hit rate is not equivalent to 20R with a 30% hit rate.

Expected value calculations:
10* 0.6 - 1 * 0.4 = 5.6
20* 0.3 - 1* 0.7 = 5.3

Don’t maximize risk-reward. Maximize expected value.

Expected value is the only metric that matters if you want to maximize your earnings over time.

The law of large numbers ensures returns move toward the expected value.

text:
💡Why Breakerblocks work? 

Market makers (MMs) and institutions often use iceberg orders to hide their size. Imagine it like an algorithm that wants to sell 1 million but starts by selling 10k every minute. 

Their main job is to create the necessary counterparty liquidity within that area, either by continuously stopping out retail traders through Wyckoff, 3-Drive, or Head & Shoulders patterns, or by using forced liquidations. 

That’s why price often starts distributing within order blocks (OBs). It’s a mechanism to bait retail into opening positions into their iceberg orders.  

However, once MMs decide there’s more to gain from going higher, they simply push through the area of the iceberg algorithm. If the algo is meant to distribute 1 million but is only selling 10k a minute, most of the liquidity will stay intact if the price pushes through fast enough.  

Now, if price pushes through and leads to a break of structure, it means MMs aren’t interested in the liquidity that a swing failure pattern (SFP) might provide to fill their shorts, they show intention to push higher.  

If price retraces back into the previously ignored area of the iceberg algorithm, it activates again after price enters the BB. 

The main misconception is that bullish BBs don’t provide buying pressure. 

They provide the opportunity of counterparty liquidity that MMs can use to fill their new capital injections, using the sell volume to fill their longs. In essence, they are converting or recycling old orders to align with their new intentions.

That’s also how SFPs work: they don’t create buy volume at a bottom. They create sell volume that MMs can use to fill their orders.  

Only OBs themselves add buying or selling pressure due to unfilled orders from the past.

That’s just a theory. I’m open to your suggestions or improvements.

What did MT mean with VSA analysis?

Imagine the entire market as a massive order book (DOM) filled with limit orders of different sizes at different prices.

Movement between these levels is lead by the delta of market orders. If market orders are strong enough, they absorb the limit orders and push to the next price level until for example buyers are exhausted, allowing sellers to take over and push through the limit orders below. It is a constant game of ping-pong between these limits/liquidity.

It is widely assumed that market makers use mostly limit orders to avoid slippage and lower transaction fees. While heatmaps can visualize this liquidity, the data is often manipulative. 

Limit orders are often cancelled moments before the price touches them, also known as spoofing.

If market makers decide to pull their limit orders, the price will dump until it hits a new wall of liquidity below that begins absorbing the market selling. (e.g. Oct 10)

Market makers sometimes increase liquidity (limit orders) at certain Key Levels while market orders attempt to push through without success. This creates CVD divergences, which are basically the same as the VSA analysis MT once mentioned. It signals MM involvement and the absorption of retail orders by them.

Images by @goldenpocketxbt

text:
Important:

CVD = Cumulative Volume Delta. 

It shows the development of the sum of the deltas (buy market orders − sell market orders) across consecutive candles. 

Let’s say it starts at 0 and the next candle has a delta of −50. Then the CVD decreases by 50, so the new CVD is −50. If the next candle’s delta is −10, the CVD decreases again, from −50 to −60.

⚠️ Why do visual candlestick patterns like OB/BBs even work? 

To understand the logic behind these, one must understand how volume is created within a chart. 

In the past, before retail traders had access to precise volume data, Time Price Opportunity (TPO) charts were used to approximate volume. 

For volume to occur, price needs to be present. Volume then shows the participation in trade at those levels. 

The presence of price and the time spent there is a limiting factor for Market Makers to get their large orders filled. The less time spent at a level, the less participation (volume) is possible. 

Looking at an example of an extended TPO profile, one can notice that it closely imitates a 30-minute candlestick chart, simply without any wicks.

Now, to approximate the volume at different prices, these 30-minute candles are added up horizontally to create a profile. 

Using this profile, one can identify where price spent most of its time and probably transacted most of its volume. Looking at the image below, one can clearly see the overlap between the TPO Profile (blue/white) on the left and the Volume Profile on the right.

The TPO profile also shows where price spent the least amount of time through single prints. 

These are areas where, by adding up all blocks horizontally, there is only one block in width. Those are often either wicks (tails = 3 single prints) or FVGs that are commonly used as S/R levels. (last image)

So, why do candlestick patterns even work? 
When we use them, we are essentially doing the same thing as analyzing a profile: we are identifying areas where many time-blocks overlap.

That is why MT also focuses mainly on the candle body rather than the wicks. A basic OB on a HTF shows a summary of multiple low-TF candle bodies that spent a lot of time within that area. 

This presence at a price level is often created by MMs trying to fill large orders, which translates directly into volume. A BB is similar, except that price previously spent a lot of time forming an OB, which then gets ignored by printing single prints/FVG. Similarly, refining works on the same principle by narrowing it down to the highest density of bodies.

text:
⚠️ How to Filter Out Weak Order Blocks

In the past, I compared OB/BB to a Time Price Opportunity chart. If we know that price spent six months within a very small range, we can approximate where most of the liquidity is located. 

Image 1:
However, with an OB where the wicks are disproportionately larger than the order block itself, using only the candle body might distort that. The wicks show the wide range in which price spent those six months. If we choose the candle body as a key liquidity level, the chance that the volume is actually in the wicks increases.

Image 2: 
On the other hand, if we go down to the 5 month timeframe, we might see an order block with almost no wicks. When there are very small wicks, we can be more confident that most liquidity is concentrated within the body of the candle. In that case, we know that price spent roughly five months within that narrow range.  

Observing how price reacted, the 5 month block seemed to work better. In MTC, we might describe this as price taking all the liquidity hidden in the wicks.

That’s also why order blocks tend to work better when they align with the POC — because that alignment might correct for any distortions caused by wick extremes.

When refining order blocks, we also check multiple timeframes to find overlapping levels that confirm that price spent the most time within a specific range, which increases the probability of it being a key market maker zone.

It’s just a theory I’m still working on, but I wanted to share my current thoughts.

What do you think of this theory? 

I haven’t done enough backtesting yet, but from a logical standpoint, it seems to make sense. 

Of course, candle closes themselves also show institutional bias, and MT also says that volume is located within the body.

However, he then also refines the wicks into bodies, choosing the areas where most of them overlap.

Order Block Blueprint

There are different levels of strength to them.

Validation: The green candle body is bigger than the red candle body.

Strength criteria:
1. Close above the previous candle’s (wick) high, indicating a BOS on the lower timeframe.

2. Break of structure confirming a trend change.

3. FVG formation, giving confidence in market maker involvement.

Additional criteria:
1. Formed during an SFP or within a higher-timeframe liquidity block.
(+ Internal sweep before OB formation.
This makes the OB similar to a Wyckoff Model 2)

2. Range Extreme: Extreme Discount/Premium

3. Refinable: We want as many bodies—and therefore as much volume—as possible to overlap within our higher-timeframe OB zone. Wicks should be smaller relative to the candle body because they can hide lower-timeframe candle bodies.

Institutional trading volume is concentrated at the bodies. Wicks can many times be printed in 1 second.

Why do we refine?

Refinable means that we go through different timeframes to identify Orderblocks on them too.

Volume is usually within the candle bodies rather than the wicks.
 
Wicks can happen within seconds, but on higher timeframes this doesn't always have to apply.

If we find a monthly Orderblock which, when we try to refine it, shows that most bodies are within the wick, then our thesis of liquidity being within the Monthly Orderblock isn't confirmed.

Imagine it like this: price starts at 1 at the start of the month, jumps up to 10 on the second day, spends the whole month there, but shortly before the close it drops, let's say, to 2.

PA on the monthly would show a candle body between 1 and 2, while the PA above would be shown as a wick.

So refining basically means simply confirming where price spent its time.

Different timeframes will show different closes. When we go on the weekly and see that most bodies are within the wick, the monthly is clearly invalidated. But then we can check where within those weekly levels most bodies, and therefore liquidity, might be located.

As MT says, "Institutional trading volume is concentrated at the bodies." We are simply double-checking by refining to avoid anomalies.

I see breaker blocks from an orderflow perspective as a zone of trapped traders. The FVG itself shows that price moved through the OB, giving those traders not much time to exit. 

There could also be traders that try to double done at the OB at the first retest (can usually be seen by lower TF OB closer to the FVG) but get offside when the FVG moves through so a FVG provides multiple opportunities for traders to get offside and later be used as counterparty.

Now when price returns to that area those traders can finally exit at BE and provide the fill to bigger players betting on continuation. I picture OB as High Volume Nodes that get revisited to provide a counterparty an entry/exit if they get ignored someone didn't want to use them for that purpose but when moving through the other side within the OB gets into negative PNL and after a restest closes to exit at BE. That's how Breakerblocks switch between bullish and bearish.  However price also often wicks into OBs nearby so everything depends on how big the player wants to get filled.

Then FVGs themselves are also areas at which players that wanted to get filled got skipped during the move and now get another chance to jump into the trend. It might also provide an opportunity for market makers to rebalance at the lows of the newly formed ranged and rebalance the inventory that they had to absorb during the move up. 

I am still digging especially the FVG part itself is very ambigious at the moment it's just a theory I try to build around it based on all the players incentives. 

My assumption is simply that candle sticks approximate a footprint chart and I try to translate those orderflow concepts into Price Action trading.

I usually don’t take ranges that seriously.

For me, it is rather simple market structure that defines my range.

In an uptrend, you’re basically seeing continuously new ranges being created, or price going sideways, deviating, and retesting previous ranges, or deviating the new SH/SL.

Most rules make it too difficult and distracting.

I’d rather simplify it down to the basic mechanics behind it: stops getting hunted (SFP) and supply and demand, like order blocks and (n)POC, being retested.

For me, Wyckoff doesn’t need to be unnecessarily complex.

I simply trade either the SFP or the retest of an OB formed during an SFP, or similar cases. That’s usually the logic that forms the Wyckoff pattern on the chart.

I don’t limit myself to a narrow framework. I mostly just observe the reaction within my level to decide whether I should enter.

That’s all you really need to know about Wyckoff. It’s basically the interaction of stop hunts, order blocks, and market structure.

I don’t really care if it fits the textbook definition of Wyckoff. I simply trade the market structure range, whether we are trending or ranging. 

This is at least my own approach to it, that works for me.

text:
With alts I look often at the ALT/BTC chart to see which one is more probable to outperform. They can be very useful to decide which asset to use for hedges.

However BTC should always be prioritized. If BTC is at supply and starts selling off Alts will follow in most cases. There can be exceptions, if there are aggressive positions in those alts that will first get squeezed. The levels can give small reactions but not very big profits so one has to be very careful trading against BTC's trend.

My approach is to simply put BTC first and then use alts if they align. Because they are mostly leveraged positions of BTC.

Back to your example where BTC is at 1H supply but 4H Demand.

In this case I would monitor BTC for its MS and how price acts around the 1H resistance if I see it holding market structure, trendlines holding and order flow is convincing for a breakout. 

Then I might attempt a tight long on the altcoin even if it is in a range. Because it might be an assymentrical bet on a breakout. I might  simply attempt it as a small scalp of the 1H support that might develop into a swing if all conditions align.

However one has to be able to adapt fast and trail stops and TP1 just in case. It might become more difficult. Try to first trade BTC profitably and only then add Altcoins on top.
